questions.question: A hoodie costs $50. Coupon A takes $10 off the price. Coupon B takes 10% off the price. Which coupon saves more money?
options: Coupon A, since 10% of $50 is $5, under $10
They tie, since 10% off $50 means taking $10 off
Coupon B, since 10% off $50 means saving $45
Coupon B, since a percent sale always beats $10
questions.explain: Turn the percent into dollars first: 10% of $50 is $5, so the $10 coupon saves twice as much. The usual trap is reading 10% as if it meant $10.

questions.question: A pair of runners costs $60. The store hands out a $15 coupon, and a sign beside the shoes says 25% off. Which deal saves more?
options: The 25% off, since it saves $25 on the shoes
They save the same, since 25% of $60 is $15
The 25% off, since it saves $45 on the shoes
The $15 coupon, since dollars beat percents
questions.explain: Change 25% into dollars: 25% of $60 is $15, exactly what the coupon takes, so it is a tie. Reading 25% as $25, or calling the $45 sale price the saving, both hide the tie.

questions.question: A board game is priced at $80. You may use a $20 coupon, or instead take 20% off. Which choice saves more?
options: The 20% off, since 20% off $80 saves $64
They are equal, since 20% off means $20 off
The $20 coupon, since 20% of $80 is only $16
The 20% off, since percents give a deeper cut
questions.explain: Work out 20% of $80 = $16, then compare it with the $20 coupon, so the coupon wins by $4. The $64 is the price you still pay, not the amount saved.

questions.question: A bike helmet costs $150. You can use a $12 coupon, or take 10% off. Which deal saves more, and how much do you save with it?
options: 10% off the helmet, which saves $135
The $12 coupon, as 10% of $150 is $1.50
The $12 coupon, since 10% is $10 off
10% off the helmet, which saves $15
questions.explain: Find 10% of $150 by moving the decimal one place to get $15, which beats the $12 coupon. Remember $135 is the price left to pay, not the saving.

questions.question: A $9 coupon and a 15% discount are both offered on the same item. At which price would the two deals save exactly the same amount?
options: A price of $60
A price of $51
A price of $24
A price of $135
questions.explain: They tie when 15% of the price equals $9, so the price is $9 divided by 0.15, which is $60; check that 15% of $60 is $9. Adding 9 and 15 as though the percent were dollars gives $24, the classic slip.

questions.question: Nadia wants to know whether a $6 coupon or 12% off saves more on a $45 board game. Which calculation answers her question directly?
options: Find $45 - 0.12 x $45 and compare with $6
Find 0.12 x $45 and compare that with $6
Compare $12 with $6, since 12% means $12
Find $45 divided by 12 and compare it to $6
questions.explain: To compare two savings they must both be in dollars, so work out 0.12 x $45 = $5.40 and set it against the $6 coupon. Subtracting first gives the sale price, which is not a saving.

questions.question: The same jacket is $75 at both stores. Store A takes $16 off with a coupon. Store B takes 20% off. Which store leaves the lower price to pay?
options: Store B, since 20% off takes $20 off the price
Store B, since 20% off gives a discount of $60
Store A, since $16 beats the $15 that 20% takes
Store B, since a percent sale always beats coupons
questions.explain: 20% of $75 is $15, so the $16 coupon takes off more and leaves $59 instead of $60. Reading 20% as $20, or calling the $60 sale price the discount, both flip the answer.

questions.question: A tablet case bundle costs $120. The choices are an $18 coupon or 12% off. How much more does the better deal save than the other one?
options: The 12% off wins, by $87.60 more
The 12% off wins, by $14.40 more
The coupon wins, by $6.00 more
The coupon wins, by $3.60 more
questions.explain: Turn the percent into dollars first: 12% of $120 is $14.40, then $18 - $14.40 = $3.60. The $105.60 is the price left to pay, so using it as the saving gives a wildly large gap.

questions.question: A hoodie is $45. Maya can use a $9 coupon or take 20% off. She says the 20% off is better because 20 is bigger than 9. Judge her thinking.
options: She is wrong: 20% of $45 is $9, so they tie
She is right, since 20% off takes $20 off the tag
She is right, since 20% off saves the $36 left
She is wrong, since coupons always beat percents
questions.explain: Compare dollars with dollars: 20% of $45 is $9, the same as the coupon, so neither deal wins. Setting the bare number 20 against 9 treats a percent as if it were dollars.

questions.question: Ravi puts a $34 book and a $36 puzzle in his cart. He may use one deal on the whole bill: a $12 coupon, or 15% off. Which deal saves more?
options: 15% off, since it saves $15 on the whole bill
The $12 coupon: 15% of $70 is only $10.50
15% off, since 15 is greater than the 12
15% off, since it takes $59.50 off the bill
questions.explain: Add the cart first ($34 + $36 = $70), then find 15% of $70 = $10.50, which is less than the $12 coupon. The $59.50 is what you would still pay, not the saving.

questions.question: A shop lets you take either $10 off or 20% off one single item, but never both. For which purchase is the 20% off the better deal?
options: A $40 game, since 20% off takes $20 off
A $45 bag, since 20% off leaves $36 saved
A $65 jacket, since 20% of it is $13
A $30 shirt, since 20% beats any coupon
questions.explain: The 20% only wins once 20% of the price passes $10, which happens above $50, and 20% of $65 is $13. On a $45 bag the saving is just $9, since $36 is the price left to pay.

questions.question: A camping tent is $90. Deal 1 is a $28 coupon. Deal 2 is 30% off. Which deal is better, and what is the final price?
options: 30% off, since $30 beats $28: price $60
30% off, so the price paid is just $27
30% off, since $63 is less than $62
The $28 coupon, so the price is $62
questions.explain: Turn 30% into dollars: 30% of $90 is $27, which is less than the $28 coupon, so the coupon leaves the lower price of $62 instead of $63. Reading 30% as $30 makes the sale look better than it really is.
